title: Red-Eye Flights: 26 Years of US Data, by Airline, Airport and Hour | ChampionTraveler
text: Red-Eye Flights: 26 Years of US Data, by Airline, Airport and Hour | ChampionTraveler # Red-Eye Flights Are a Western Phenomenon: 26 Years of Data on Who Flies Overnight, From Where, and When Updated November 10, 2026, first published September 9, 2026 by ChampionTraveler Only about 1 in 60 US domestic flights is a red-eye, and 97% of them take off in the West. In 2025 the reporting airlines operated 6,898,743 domestic flights; 115,580 of them were overnight flights, scheduled to leave between 9 pm and 3 am and land between 3 am and 10 am the next morning. 97% departed from the thirteen Pacific and Mountain states, Alaska and Hawaii. In 26 years of data that share has never been below 95%. Nobody had put a number on the west-to-east shape of overnight flying before; this study does, and it follows it back to 2000. The red-eye is not fading. There were 75,158 in 2000 and 115,580 in 2025, a 54% increase, and as a share of the major airlines’ flights it rose from 1.37% to 2.28%. What changed is who flies them, from where, and at what hour. Each section below carries one number a reader can take away, the chart behind it, and the years it covers. ## Red-eyes are a western phenomenon A red-eye works in one direction. Leave the West Coast at 11 pm, cross three time zones, and land in New York or Boston at 7 am with a business day ahead; the reverse trip has no overnight slot that makes sense. That geometry is the whole map: 97% of 2025’s red-eyes departed from the western states, and among the 300 busiest red-eye routes, 82% land in the Central or Eastern time zones. 66,920 red-eyes, 58% of the total, flew 2,000 miles or more. | State | Red-eye departures | Share of all US red-eyes | | --- | --- | --- | | California | 44,266 | 38.3% | | Nevada | 15,958 | 13.8% | | Hawaii | 12,129 | 10.5% | | Washington | 11,580 | 10.0% | | Arizona | 8,194 | 7.1% | | Alaska | 6,072 | 5.3% | | Colorado | 5,821 | 5.0% | | Utah | 4,611 | 4.0% | | Oregon | 3,557 | 3.1% | | Puerto Rico | 2,107 | 1.8% | | Texas | 368 | 0.3% | | New Mexico | 175 | 0.2% | | New York | 167 | 0.1% | | American Samoa (Pago Pago) | 148 | 0.1% | | Idaho | 147 | 0.1% | | Illinois | 113 | 0.1% | ## 26 years of red-eyes Two lines because the answer depends on the denominator. The Bureau of Transportation Statistics expanded the set of airlines that must report in 2018, which added millions of regional flights that almost never fly overnight, so the all-airline share dips that year for a reporting reason. On a consistent set of the major airlines and the carriers they absorbed, the red-eye share climbed from 1.37% in 2000 to 2.28% in 2025, peaking at 2.42% in 2018. The low point was 2009 (61,657 red-eyes), the collapse was 2020 (47,975), and the record is 2019 (116,850). The red-eye capitals Anchorage is the red-eye capital of America by share. 26% of every departure from Anchorage is a red-eye (22% in 2000), and Anchorage to Seattle was the busiest red-eye route in the country in 2000 and is still number two. No other large airport is above 13%. By count, Los Angeles leads with 19,064 red-eye departures in 2025, but the crown used to belong to Las Vegas: 18,583 in 2000, 14% of everything that left the airport, falling to 6,562 by 2020 and recovering to 15,409. The busiest single red-eye route is Los Angeles to New York JFK (2,337 flights in 2025); LAX to JFK peaked at 3,303 in 2019 and is down 29% since. legacy airlines lost the red-eye market. American, Delta and United, counting the airlines they absorbed, flew 97% of red-eyes in 2000 and 64% in 2025. JetBlue peaked at 15% of all red-eyes in 2011 and is at 7%; Alaska rose from 3% to 12%; Frontier and Spirit arrived in 2015. Southwest flew no overnight flights for the first 25 years of this series and took 5.6% of the market in its first year. In the twelve months to June 2026 it flew 10,361 red-eyes, 9% of every red-eye in the country, about 1,287 a month by June 2026. The national share barely moved over that year (1.64% to 1.69%) because the other airlines flew fewer: Southwest took the overnight market the others were shrinking. ## When red-eyes leave The middle-of-the-night red-eye is disappearing. Departures after midnight were 31% of red-eyes in 2000 and 14% in 2025; the 11 pm departure went from 29% to 40%. Summer is red-eye season: 1.96% of July flights are red-eyes against 1.46% in January (2015 to 2025, excluding 2020).
